title: Put Pressure On
subtitle: 「向……施壓／令……承受壓力」其實有兩個主要語義家族： 一是主動影響或迫使某人做某事；二是某種成本、工作量或情況令人／系統承受負擔。這兩類不能混為一談。
description: 「向……施壓／令……承受壓力」其實有兩個主要語義家族： 一是主動影響或迫使某人做某事；二是某種成本、工作量或情況令人／系統承受負擔。這兩類不能混為一談。

words.example: Managers should not pressurise staff to work unpaid overtime.
words.exampleZh: 管理人員不應施壓要求員工無薪加班。

exercises.original: The manager put pressure on staff to work late without extra pay.
exercises.zh: 經理施壓要求員工無額外薪酬地加班。
exercises.upgrade: A. Pressurise · 施壓；向……施加壓力

options.explanation: Pressurise ✓ — means actively put psychological or practical pressure on someone to make them act; it is especially natural in British English. In this sentence, direct interpersonal pressure to make staff act fits pressurise. That combination of force, intention and context makes Pressurise the most precise replacement.

Pressure — as a verb means try to influence or force someone towards an action or decision; it is especially common in American English. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: direct interpersonal pressure to make staff act fits pressurise.

Push — means urge someone strongly towards effort or action; it is often lighter and can be constructive. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: direct interpersonal pressure to make staff act fits pressurise.

Persuade — means change someone's mind through reasons or argument rather than pressure. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: direct interpersonal pressure to make staff act fits pressurise.

Encourage — means support or motivate someone and is generally more positive and less forceful. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: direct interpersonal pressure to make staff act fits pressurise.

Demand — means state a strong requirement; it is the request itself rather than the influence used to secure compliance. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: direct interpersonal pressure to make staff act fits pressurise.

It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: the issue is workload and resource burden rather than coercing a decision.

Place demands on ✓ — means require substantial time, effort, resources or capacity; it describes burden rather than coercion. Stress — often names a state of psychological or physical strain, not an act of influencing someone. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: the issue is workload and resource burden rather than coercing a decision.

options.explanation: Apply pressure to ✓ — is a formal way to describe deliberate influence or leverage in business, politics or negotiations. In this sentence, deliberate formal influence in a corporate context fits apply pressure. That combination of force, intention and context makes Apply pressure to the most precise replacement.

Pressurise — means actively put psychological or practical pressure on someone to make them act; it is especially natural in British English. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: deliberate formal influence in a corporate context fits apply pressure.

Lean on — is an informal idiom for using personal influence or leverage to pressure someone. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: deliberate formal influence in a corporate context fits apply pressure.

Push — means urge someone strongly towards effort or action; it is often lighter and can be constructive. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: deliberate formal influence in a corporate context fits apply pressure.

Persuade — means change someone's mind through reasons or argument rather than pressure. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: deliberate formal influence in a corporate context fits apply pressure.

Encourage — means support or motivate someone and is generally more positive and less forceful. It is related to influence or burden, but it misses an important part of this context: deliberate formal influence in a corporate context fits apply pressure.

falseSynonyms.zh: 鼓勵 ≠ put pressure on encourage 通常是正面支持，並保留較大選擇空間。
falseSynonyms.point: ENGLISH COMPARISON Encouragement is weaker and more supportive.

falseSynonyms.zh: 說服 ≠ pressure persuade 是透過理由令對方自願改變想法，不必有壓力。
falseSynonyms.point: ENGLISH COMPARISON Persuasion relies on reasons rather than pressure.

falseSynonyms.zh: 要求 ≠ put pressure on demand 是提出強硬要求；pressure 是影響對方接受要求的過程。
falseSynonyms.point: ENGLISH COMPARISON A demand is a request/requirement, not the pressure itself.

falseSynonyms.zh: 威脅 ≠ 所有 pressure threaten 是明確提出不利後果；很多 pressure 並沒有威脅。
falseSynonyms.point: ENGLISH COMPARISON Threatening is a stronger, narrower tactic.

falseSynonyms.zh: 壓力狀態 ≠ 主動施壓 stress 可指心理壓力狀態，不等於某人向另一人施壓。
falseSynonyms.point: ENGLISH COMPARISON Stress is often a condition, not an influence tactic.

falseSynonyms.zh: 負擔 ≠ 所有 pressure burden 強調負重／責任，不一定有人主動影響決定。
只在強迫 sense 接近 coerce 比一般 put pressure on 強，通常包含威脅或幾乎沒有選擇。
falseSynonyms.point: ENGLISH COMPARISON Coerce implies serious force or intimidation.

falseSynonyms.zh: 地區與詞性陷阱 pressure 可作名詞／動詞；pressurise 是英式常見動詞。
falseSynonyms.point: ENGLISH COMPARISON Check grammar and regional usage.
